The London Journals up to the 1st August announce the arrival in that capital of the ex- Regent, accompanied with the Duchess of Victory, and the favourable reception shown to them by the British Ministry, and a large circle of the most distinguished portion of the English nobility. The papers particularly notice the departure of the two French Princes on their way back to Paris ; the circumstances which may have led to this determination are gravely discussed at length in the papers, as it was generally understood that the roval Dukes contemplated spending a longer time in England. The sensation produced on the minds of the French people, appears to have been similar to that experienced iti London, if we are to judge from the spirit of the Brass in that country, the extracts furnished from the Times taken from the Sieclc, Journal des Debats, arid the Commerce, unanimously agree in stating tiiat the intelligence of the unexpected return of the young Dukes was received with general surprise and in cettain quarters with real alarm, the public being disposed to entertain the idea that the movement alluded, denoted some political contingency of an unpleasant nature, therefore unfavourable to the peaceable relation which existed between the

governments. These rumours had scarcely acquired a certain degree of publicity, when the Parisian folks were completely surprised by the announcement of the prospect of a visit from no less a personage than the Queen þÿ of the þÿIsles þÿ that the sovereign of Great Britain accompanied by twoCubinet Ministers and a limited retinue would visit 1 1 is Majesty

From the Morning Chronicle. Private Correspondence, 1 have to announce a circumstance which has for the time superseded even the interest excited by the expected arrival of Queen Victoria þÿ an event which in fact might have plunged France into the deepest dishes and

have deeply affected the interest of the whole of Europe. Yesterday the King and the greater part of the Royal Family of France had a narrow escape from destruction, indeed so narrow, that I have been told by one who witnessed it that their escape may be considered miraculous. It appears that the King, the Queen, the Count de Paris, the Prince de Joinville, and the Duke þÿD Aumale and in fact all the members of the Royal Family now here, yesterday took one of their usual drives in the neighbourhood of the Chateau The carriage occupied by the Royal Family was a large open one, bung around with curtains with seats across it, and capable of carrying a great number of persons. It is called 1 believe a þÿ Char a þÿBanc and is not unlike the pleasure vans so common in our metropolis. To show its great size I need only mention that the carriage I speak of contained upon this occasion no less than ten members of the Royal Family including Louis Philippe, the Queen, and the Count de Paris ; the carriage was drawn by four very spirited horses. The party, it appears, happened in the course of their drive to pass through Tteport, a small fishing village situate two miles from this place, and it happened to be the first time the Count de Paris visited the place, the loyal inhabitants considered it their duty to do their future Sovereign special honour on the occasion, and they accordingly saluted H. K. H. with a "feu de þÿjoie, the guns were fired just as the carriage was approach-

ing the neighbourhood of the bridge which spans the Brezle. a small river at the mouth of w hich the village of Treport is situated. Nothing could be more unexpected than the result. The horses, startled by the noise, commenced plunging furiously. The postillion lost all command of them and they darted forward towards the bridge, the parapet of which the leaders cleared at a bound. The third horse was dragged after its companions, and for a moment the destruction of the whole party seemed inevitable, but fortunately the postillion was enabled to acquire some command over the fourth horse, and he did not follow, Had he done so there could be no doubt as to the result. Assistance however was happily at hand, and the whole party were released from their perilous situation, not however, before the traces had been with great difficulty cut, and the horses left to their fate. The three horses of course, fell into the stream below and were injured, but the postillion escaped. I need hardly say that the alarm of the whole party in such a fearful circumstance must have been very great The Queen was much affected and wept bitterly after the danger was over. The King himself behaved with great presence of mind ; he took the voung Count of Paris in Lis arms, and refused to leave the carriage until every member of his family was placed in safety on þÿ terra finna.' You will not wonder after this detail, that an event so interesting to France and Europe in general, should for a time have superseded

GADE. A new Mozart has risen suddenly above the horizon of the musical world. He began his career as a composer by a series of simple melodies, but even in these humble eflorts he betrayed a precocious and remarkable talent, which did not escape the observation of the Danish dilettanti. It one day occurred to young Gade that he would employ himself in the composition of a symphony ; he did so, and, w hen concluded, he forwarded it, with a suitable letter to Mendelssohn, at Eeipsic. The passage of the Straits is generally considered a very difficult one, probably from reading accounts of the old navigators, some of whom w ere enabled to gel through ; hut. with a well found ship it might be easily done in from three to four days, and at a much less cost of wear and tear than in doubling the Cape, and certainly with infinitely less danger to the safety of the vessel. The idea entertained by some of supplying peat to steamers navigating the South Pacific is absurd. The labour of cutting and prepar-
ing it, with any population the Falkland Isles are likely to have, is out of the questions and even were peat a good substitute for coal, the expense of shipping it would be immense.

The Bengal Herkaru says that the Assam Tea Company propose to send to England samples of the indigenous and cultivated tea of Assam in a raw state. The leaves to be packed as taken from the trees, alter being dried, and the subsequent preparations of the lea for use to he left entirely to parties at home, where it is thought there would he no difficulty in preparing it lor consumption. The party from whom our contemporary has derived his information, seems confident that the experiment will prove successful if acted upon ; and among the advantages that would follow its realization, the foremost are þÿ India would in a short time be able to supply the demand of Great Britain for tea þÿ the leaf in its raw state might be compressed into less bulk than at present, and, bv the exclusion to a much greater extent of the atmospheric air. reach England with a higher and purer flavor. And further, it is probable that the tea introduced into England in its raw form for manufacture, would be exempted from the duty imposed upon manufactured tea. We trust that the trial may be made, and that the attempt may meet with success.

from Bell's Weekly Messenger, London August 28, 1843. COMMERCIAL PROSPECTS AT HONG KONG. The subjoined account of this newlv ac quired island, and the cheering accounts which the writer gives of our commercial prospects in China, will be read with consid erable interest. The letter is dated Macao, March 20 : þÿ " I must now give you some account of Hong Kong itself. It is not, as it has been called, a barren island ; there are many very fruitful and productive spots on it. as much by good management, probably, as will serve the inhabitants for market gardens. It is about 20 miles in circumference, and posseses the great advantage over Macao of having excellent harbours. The site chosen for Victoria, the new town, is the front of the hill, facing the harbour on the north-west side. Owing to everv one running up his house as he laneied most advantageous at the time, it is built without regularity, or that attention to effect which a Trench or Dutch colony would ex hi bit, and this is undoubtedly a great defect, but the houses are substantial and elegant, evidencing the fact that it is no speculating feverish impulse, but a settled conviction, that this island is destined to be the enterpot for the trade of an empire þÿ that is, to he the Anglo Chinese capital Government are busy forming public roads and erecting handsome buildings for their own purposes, while private houses are springing up daily with a rapidity which would piease our Yankee friends amazingly. The population is numerous, especially the Chinese, who arc here in

crowds, and have all the business in the bazaars and principal streets. They are the shopkeepers and the artisans of the settlement þÿ are verv excellent colonists þÿ they are peaceable, industrious, ar.d most obliging and civil. The English are the merchants, hotelkeepers, and seafaring part, and are both numerous and respectable, We have already three religious places of worship here, one a building allotted for tne present to the Church of England until a more suitable one can be erected, one Baptist church, and one belonging to the Church of tiome, several ol whose missionaries have arrived here, and are very active 5 there is a kind of college, I believe, attached to the chapel. I suppose they hope to occupy their lost ground in the country through which the disciples ol L.oyola once pieaclied without hindrance, and some of whom even held posts about the imperial person. The trade is rapidly increasing, and now that all doubt about our retaining Hong Kong is removed, it will continue to do so far more rapidly still. A newspaper is published once a week ; a second had started, but failed ; in fact everything goes on as well as the most sanguine friends of the settlement could wish; and those who saw Hong Kong when the British flag was first hoisted, two veais and six months ago, can only tell the extent of the change. Then there was not a hut on it, now it is covered with warehouses and private dwellings ; at that time a few miserable fishing boats occupied iis magnifi-

cent harbour, now it is covered with the tall masts ol stately ships, whose colours prove thev come from every pai l of the globe, all busy trading, while the emblem ol England's sovereignty proudly floats on the hill above, giving safety and protection to them all. MORNING CHRONICLE September 1st ( From the CnnstiMionnel .) The approaching visit of Queen Victona to France is the subject of various comtnents on the part of the Publie Press. 1 he Debuts unreservedly applaud the idea of the voyage ; other papers arc suspicious of its object, and express alarm, they suppose that the consequence of the Royal interview may be either a treaty of commerce or some other diplomatic arrangements, in which the interest of France may not be sufficiently secured. If we have not believed that a visit of the Qu"en of England to the King of the French would cement for ever the union of the two Governments, and the two Nations, wc are not the more disposed to believe that our national interest can be seriously injured by it. We have regarded the projected excursion of the young Queen as a satisfactory manifestation of our dynasty, and as friends of that dynasty we congratulate ourselves on it ; but in our eyes, the visit to Eu can have no other bearing. þÿ France and England are two countries governed by Constitutional principles, that is to say at London as at Paris, Royalty is irresponsible, and the entire action of the Government belongs to the ministers It is most certainly said, and on this perhaps with truth, thai if in the approaching interview between the two Monarchs a political arrangement, a Treaty of commerce for instance should be agreed upon, it is not the present ministers who would assign their responsibility as a reason for refusing to subscribe to the per-

sona! arrangements of the Chief <>f the State. On this point we perfectly agree with those journals which have taken alarm, we do not for a moment doubt the pusillanimity oi oar Ministers, and wo are well convinced

3W5.STS& T.ia?rnr:&33K 3S3 &53at31T®3 ATSS, that, in order to keep themselves in the good graces of Royalty, they would be willing to countersign any thing which might be preseated to them. It is not therefore, in the conduct of the ministry that we have any faith. If M. Guizot had been allowed to have his way, the treaty of commerce with England at the prospect of which the Country is so alarmed, would long since have been inflicted on it. It is not necessary for Royally to intervene to stimulate his sympathies, they are already acquired for any propositions of Lord Aberdeen; and the most ardent desire of the subscriber of the treaty of the right of search is. to add to it a treaty of commerce between France and Great Britain, this is certain, if M. Guizot hesitates, and, if he allows the projects to lay dorment it is perhaps because Royal prudence tempers his zeal, or because the remembrance of his Parliamentary chastisement on the subject of the right of search make him dread to encounter again the anger of the Chambers on a question on which they certainly do not agree with him The guarantee of French interests, and it is so strong thai it fully tranquilizes us, is, that no treaty of commerce effecting any change in the duties can receive its execution without the sanction of the Chambers, and certainly will never meet in eithei one or the other with majorities disposed to sacrifice our national manufactories to those ot England. Any minister which should attempt such a task would pertsh in the work, were it even as popular in the

Country as the present Cabinet is the reverse. The visit therefore, to the Chateau D'Eu can have none of the consequences that are apprehended from it, and we can allow ourselves to approve of it without a fear that we should hereafter have to deploie the high price we had to pay lor the gracious visit of Queen Victoria.
From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London August 21, 1843. THE LATE DESTRUCTIVE STORMS

We regret to state that the accounts which have reached us from various parts of the country fully confirm the statements which we gave last week of the damage done by the terrific storms of the9th instant. Amongst the most serious sufferers, besides those we have already noticed, the holders of property on the Bedfordshire leval may be mentioned. In the fens alone, it is said upwards of 20!>0 acres of the hay crop, of the value of at least 10,000/. have been totally destroyed, and the pasturage of 1000 head of cattle entirely inundated The consequence of this sad disaster is, that about 1000 persons, men, women, and children, have been thrown out of employment. On the estate of Upper Upham, in the parish ot Aldbourn, Wilts, the property of Mi. J Round, M. P. for Maldon. occupied hv Mr. Church; the crops of corn were damaged by the hailstones to the extent of nearly 1000/- : 90 acres ol w heat. 54 acres of barley, 35 acres of oats, and 20 acres of peas and veiehes were literally thrashed sttch a scene of devastation has been rarely witnessed The ctops on the adjoining farm, occupied hv Mr. Deudmon, also sustained considerable damage. A correspondent at Churchill, Oxfordshire, has sent us a rrost afflicting account of the damage done bv the storm in that pait of the couniry. At Churchill, he says, the detune

tion of corn (which Is compleieL- beaten out) and of glass, cannot amount to less than 3000/ ; at Chipping- Norton, 40 0/.; Over- Norton, 2o00/. ; and Eathrop, 1000/. Before the storm the Corn crop was a very good one. What is left is a fair crop ; about three bushels to the acre shed out. While mentioning this part of the country, it affords us considerable gratification to slate, on the authority of a tenant of Mr. Langston, M. P., that that gentleman, in the kindest manner, and without solicitation, called on those tenants who were the greatest sufferers, and generously gave lOOOh, to be divided in proportion to itre loss sustained by each indivi dual. We sincerely hope that the liberal example thus set by Mr. Langston may be followed by every landlord whose estate may be within the range of this awful visitation. Another corresp indent, after giving an account of the fearful ravages of the storm, says : þÿ " And now let me direct your atlen. tion to the loss of the farmer. Pounds are but little things here, and hundreds tell up but slowly the amount : thousands upon thousands multiply upon our calculation, while we look on those fields which only a few days ago presented some of the fairest crops and most promising appearances that our eyes have long beheld, reduced to such a state of desolation as to be worth little more than for fodder or manure This overwhelming loss must be severely felt by many, while to some it presents nothing less than the stern features and fearful prospect of utter ruin þÿ

unless as I sincerely hope will be the case, the wealthy and tiie benevolent, with that promptitude and charitable assistance which has never been appealed to in vain, should kindly and opportunely prevent it." On Tuesday morning several parts of the suburbs were visited by a violent storm, which commenced in such a manner as to excite the most serious and alarming apprehensions. At Clapham the first intimation given was by a violent peal of thunder, at.d vivid flashes of lightning from the south-west, followed immediately by torrents of rain and hail, which fell with tremendous force, and speedily inundated the whole of Claphamcommon and the waste lands in that vicinity, besides inflicting a great deal of damage among the hothouses, and other buildings of similar construction. The depth of the water covering Clapham and Wandsworth commons became at last so great, that many persons, who were compelled by business to be in town at a certain hour, were forced to be conveyed in carts to the high roads. In many places the horses drawing omnibuses and other vehicles were up to their knees in water. From the low lands of Wandsworth a curious view was beheld The clouds, apparently almost resting on the chimney-pots of the metropolis, produced a s <rt of mirage, which threw the higher buildings of London into an artificial light, presenting the picture of an aerial city. Much damage was done bv the floods to the houses situate in the Claphutn and Brixton roads. The mid. and counties wete also visited by storn s>

which, in severity, were not much less than those of the preceding week. At Birmingham, on Tuesday night, the lightning was most vivid, and the rain descended for some hours in torrents. Along the Derby fine ot railway the rivers were much flooded. In most places the wheal was again neuter, down, and where it was fit for the sickle was much damaged. Such a succession of stortnf is said to have been almost unprecedented.

Among the " fond memorials" which Louis Philippe presented to Queen Victoria, whose visit seems to have filled His Majesty with delight, were two splendid specimens of Gobelins tapestry, which were brought down from Paris for the inspection of ller Majesty ; the subjects represented on these pieces of tapestry, are saidto he. From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London September 11, 1843. Sp.\tn. þÿ The accounts from tins unhappy country are just such as we anticipated. In Madrid there is a very general feeling of hostility to the present government, and it has been determined to make a search tor the arms which have been concealed by the National Guards A mutiny "f the Princeza regiment broke out, but was soon suppressed; and several of the parties summarily executed. The particulars of the affair will he found in our last page. It will he seen by the subjoined intelligence, which we have received this morning, that the work of anarchy and bloodshed is fearfully progressing at Barcelona : þÿ REVOLUTIONARY" MOVEMENT AT BARCELONA. " Perpignan, Sept 6. þÿ For some days past a movement appeared to be preparing at Barcelona. Some free corps who had been refused admission into the town succeeded in entering, and joined the rioters who guarded the approach to the square of the municipality. The garrison did not quit the citadel. On the morning of the 2d the 3d battalion of volunteers revolted, and were joined by another battalion ot volunteers quartered at the Atarrnzanas. These þÿ battalions proclaimed the central junta. two Biera was appointed commander in chief On the 3d, at seven o'clock in the evening, there was a first engagement between some companies of the line com.ng from 1 arrogona Mid the volunteers, who wished to prevent them from entering the citadel. rI he volunteers were repulsed with a loss of 15 wounded þÿ The popular committee formed itseif

into a supreme junta. On the night of the 3d, Brigadiers l'rim and Blanco, at the head o! the Regiment of the Constitution, had taken possession of Barcelonetta, and at six o'clock in the morning of the 4tn a lusillade commenced between them and the volunteers, which lasted until night. The citadel fired several rounds of grape shot. Col. Baiges, >he President of the Junta, was killed. The insurgents had 100 men hers de, combat. At six o'clock in the evening Prim attacked the Gate del Angel, where a captain of the insurgents was killed. The firing re commenced next morning, and still continued at five o'clock p. m., when the courier started, particnlarlv on the side of the sea gate. Don Rafael de Gollada has been appointed president of the junta, and that assembly has issued a proclamation calling to arms the people of Catalonia and Spain, and urging them to demand the convocation of a centra! junta. The junta has decreed the penalty of death against evcrv individual who should ttUuck its principles."

A copy following curious letter, in which Queen Pomare, of Tahiti, solicits the protection of the English government against France, has been received in the city : þÿ " Tahiti, Jan. 23. 1843. þÿ M v dear Friend mid Sister Queen V ictoria, Queen of Great Britain, þÿ Health and peace to you, and saved may you bo hv Jehovah, the foundation of our power as Queens of our respective countries. We dwell in peaee from the arrangements made by our predecessors.

!t>Xx£ ' This is mv speech to you, my sister fi ieiid. Commisserate ine iri my affliction, in my helplessness, and in the difficulties in which my nation is involved with Fiance. Our intelligence from the disturbed districts consists principally of accounts of public meetings, which are being held almost daily, in which the farmers and others discuss thfcir grievances; and at which petitions have hecn agreed on, in some instances calling on parliament to provide a remedy, and in others, soliciting her Majesty to dissolve the present parliament. The only outrage that has come to our knowledge is contained in the following letter from Swansea: þÿ Swansea, Wednesday night þÿ Some few days since the Minke gate, having hern destroyed, & the toll-house partially pulled down, and it being determined to rebuild it, the necessary timber with several hundred bricks and slates were sent to Llanelly, and on Monday morning tetnoved to the site of the ruined toll -house; such, however, was the "feeling manifested on the part ot the inhabitants, that no one would sell the builder a single bushel of Lime, no man would assist in the work, nor would they even supply him with water to slack the lime. This being the case, the builder returned to Llanelly to got Lime, and brought up a butt of water, leaving the slates, bricks, &c , at Minke. Upon his return, however, he found lhat the walls of the toll-house which had Lean standing were levelled with the ground. Onlv 2 bricks were left out of 500. The whole of the slates, 800 in number, were broken into small pieces, and the timber destroyed. 1 am sorry to say that in the course of last night the farm, with the outhouses,

stacks of corn, &e.. in fact the whole ot the stock, &c., of a farm, about two miles from (Jwm Neath, were burnt down. 1 have not, however, as yet been able to ascertain whether it was an incendiary fire or not. The property i9 of very considerable value.

Foreign Intei.mgi-.nce. þÿ The French government is busily occupied in endeavorin'; to give satisfaction to the French merchants and manufacturers by taking into its consideration the present state of French trade arid commerce. The contest between those interested in the French West India colonies, and the growers of beet root in France þÿ or, in other words, the French farmers þÿ still continues to embarrass the council and cabinet of Louis Philippe. The French farmers make a common cause with the beet-root growers, and insist that the encouragement of the growth of this article is necessary for the protection of French agriculture, and particularly at a time when the French corn has become so reduced in price that the conversion of the beet- root lands into corn lands would complete the ruin of French agriculture. This party has been too strong for the government; and M. Guizot has been compelled to give way to the landed interest, and to abandon the greater portion of the increased tax which he was about to propose upon beet- root. We observe in the French papers two articles worthy of notice, because they show that the same causes, as respects interior trade, and the condition of the working classes, arc operating in France as in England. The papers complain, that whilst the harvest is so abundant, and the exportation of French coin is every day proceeding, bread is still rising in price in Paris, whilst it is everywhere declining in the provinces. The other paragraph expresses its astonish-

ment and regret at the decreased consumption of þÿbutcher meat s in Paris, The papers attribute this to the diminished means of the lower classes, whose condition it was apprehended would be anything hut improved in the approaching winter, from the general failing off of the interior trade. Put the vintage, it is said, has turned out as favourable as the harvest, and the wines in the south are everywhere of the first quality. There is one article in the Portuguese papers which deserves a passing mention. They announce the conclusion of the commercial treaty between Great Britain and Portugal. '1 his intelligence had alarmed the merchants of Madrid, a deputation of whom had called on M. Lopez, and expressed their apprehensions ot the consequences of such a treaty to Spanish trade. The ministry, it appears, immediately forwarded dispatches on the subject to M. Saucho, the Spanish minister in London. In Spain, the elections for the new Cortes have terminated, mid l ho Cortes is to be opened within a few days. The National Guard of Madrid is to he called out to receive and welcome the new parliament. In the confusion of party accounts it is very difficult to anticipate what will be the character ol the majority of these Chambers. In the mean iimo several of the great towns and cities have declared against the government, mid have established a correspondence with the junta at Bircelona.

Narrow Escape of the Town of Cove fhoai Bombardment. þÿ The last number of the Cork Reporter contains the following extraordinary statement: þÿ For some time past we have been in possession of facts relative to the Commander of one of her Majesty's vessels lately lying at Cove, which tvere of so startling arid extraordinary a nature, that, though well authenticated at the time, we withheld the publication of them, lest our informant might have been mistaken However, all doubt has now been cleared up upon the subject, one of our reporters having had the facts repeated to him very recent I v bv an authority that cannot be disputed. They are these " While her Majesty's brig the Lynx, a vessel mounting three guns of formidable calibre, but pierced for ten, was lying off Cove, her commander, Captain Burs'em, one day gave the order to clear the deck for action! The order was quicklv obeyed, the drums beat to quarters, the three guns were primed and loaded, in fact, double shotted, and the crew waited in breathless silence and astonishment for what was to follow ; but they were not long kept in suspense, for in a few minutes after Captain Burslem ordered the guns to be fired upon the town ! The officers next in command were horror-struck at hearing such an order and though feeling the tremendous risk they would, under almost any other circumstances, run by interfering with the order of their captain, yet they clearly saw that they would be lully justified in preventing the execution

of an order by which perhaps thousands of her Majesty's peaceable subjects would be hurled to destruction in the midst of the most profound tranquility and peace. Accordingly the first lieutenant and one or two of the other officers consulted for a moment, and having arrived at the conclusion that no such order could bv any possibility have been given bv any man in his senses, they contrived to induce the captain to go below for a moment and suspend the order ; this he complied with, and having been got into his own cabin, every precaution was taken to secure him, and the whole affair reported to the Admiral. Captain Burslem was immediately removed, antl the Lynx is now under the command of her first lieutenant. It has been stated that on two or three occasions of late Captain Lurslem had evinced symptoms of impaired intellect, but never before to such an extent."

Light þÿGold. In consequence of the recent!) issued proclamation respecting light gold, many of the bankers and shopkeepers have determined to deduct a fixed sum for every gold coin that may be deficient in weight, without reference to tfte amount of such deficiency. In some cases the deduction is fixed at 2d., which may, perhaps, be re garded as a fair average of the deficiency ; in other cases, as the bankers of Essex, the deduction is, we believe, fixed at about 7d. ; but the amount, whatever it may be, is in most cases, a completely arbitrary one; ana, as usual, ihe public will be the sufferers. There can be but little doubt that much of the light gold coin received hv some parties during the late weighing panic ( he holders <d which vveie compelled to submit to a reduction, more especially among the poor classes) has attain been put into circulation, and the process of deducting for deficient weight on the same piece of coin may thus be carried on ad. infinitum. To remedy this it has been suggested that no person tendering any coin which upon being weighed shall fie found light should submit to any deduction lining made unless such coin be stamped or marked to such a manner as to preclude the possibility of its being again issued as a current coin. This course will effectually prevent anv fraudulent re issue, and the dealer, having taken the coin at a depreciated value, will not suffer bv liui g compelled to sell it at the Bank as bullion, but will in most cases receive sufficient

1 compensate him for the trouble of having to do so The public officers to whom such coin mav be tendered will doubtless deface u ; : þÿ but it rests with the public individually to protect themselves by some such measure as the above from the risk of having the light coin re-issued by the trader at its full value.

ALGIERS. TheFrench Minister of War publishes a despatch from Marshal Bugeaud, dated October 1 !). The marshal says : þÿ ' It is with grea' satisfaction 1 have the honor of announcing to you that we have at length seriously brought under subjection and organised the mountains of the Ouarenseris. The preceding submissions were not of a solid nature, as ihev were only made by very secondary chiefs. This time things have passed very differently. Four columns, provided with everything necessary for a prolonged sojourn invaded the East of these mountains. Not a gun was fired against that of Orleansville ; the population, on the contrary, hastened to

supply our wants, and endeavored to diminish our resentment for their twice violated promises of submission." Marshal Bugeaud then goes on to state that the other columns encountered some obstacles, but no serious resistance, and to relate accounts of interviews with different chiefs. He goes into considerable details of submissions, alter chastisement by the French troops, and gives

an account of the resistance ottered by the Belli- Ameers to Abd-el-Kader ; but tins fact has already been published. Alter these details, the marshal r.oi eludes bis despatch as follows : þÿ " 1 think 1 can now atnrui that the province of Algiers perfectly united with is that of (Jran, in the whole breauth of tbe country, fn>m the desert to the sea. Abd el- Kader may possibly return to tlie part which 1 have just pacified, and he would in such case produce some perturbation; but tie could organise nothing dangerous, for these tribes are horribly fatigued and ruined." The London papers ol the 3d contain intelligence from Alliens ol ari attempt to produce a counter revolution by General (Jolocotroni, one of the aides de camp of King Otho; his Majesty, in order to remove all suspicion of his own participation in the design, assembled his Council ol .State, together with the chief civil and military authorities, on the 1 1th of October, and addressed them in these words : þÿ " Having embraced the constitutional system, which I conscientiously believe to be necessary for the welfare and prosperity of my beloved Gicece, 1 fervently desire that q shall be established with tranquility and good order. 1 have therefore to beg of you, gentlemen, to make known to all persons in

, authority under you, to your frionds sod to your acquaintances, this tr y irrevocably Royal w ill, that no one may be deceived as to iiiv desire, and tie led awav to act, m word or deed, against tiie new system of government." The subsequent events are thus given: þÿ " Athens, Oct. 16. þÿ The above most important declaration vvas made by King Otho to an extraordinary convoked assembly of the ministers of state and other leading characters in Athens, in consequence of very serious distutbances having taken place in tfiat capital. On the 9th of October General Colocotroni, one of his Majesty's aides de camp, did all in his power to instigate a counter revolution. His attempts, however, to seduce the troops entirely failed. 'I he King pleaded ignorance of any such movement Icing attempted, and after some hesitation consented to dismiss tbe obnoxious aide de <amp. who was then sentenced bv the government to quit the country forthwith. He decided ori embarking in the Austrian pneket, which was on the ooinl of sailing lor 1 riestc, but the populace had become so exasperated against him, that on his arriving at the Pirams harbor they attacked the carriage, and would have probably sacrificed him on the spot, had not the coachman lashed his horses into a gallop, and at fu 1 speed returned to the capital. "Once more he essayed to reach the har" hour with a strong escort of cavalry, but tbe populace were too determined, and actually forced tliem back again. Finally, he suc-

ceeded in getting on board the Greek government steamer, by embarking at a distant part of the shore, and reached JSyrn. "Four days after the above event, a very large body of the people prevented Monsieur Rhalli, the laie obnoxious minister of justice, from embarking on board tbe Austrian steamer. On this oceasiott the military succeeded in dispersing the crowd, without causing bloodshed, and Monsieur Rhalli was saved from popular vengeance bv the French n inisier, who conveyed hint in bis own carriage to the harbour, and there placed bint in safety on board the French war steamer Tattare, which conveyed him to Andres. "Since the King's speech on the 14th the capital has remained quiet, and I feci persuaded that if his Majesty will only act with sincerity, and not be led away bv designing hangers on, the Greeks reall v wish his continuance on the throne, and will cordially lend their support to carrying out the new order of things.

From Dell's Weekly Messenger, London November 6, 1843. The principal item of intelligence from India is an insurrection at Lahore, and the murder of Shere Singh, his son Purlaub Singh, and all their families, on t lie 15th of September. Tins fearful massacre was brought about bv a band of conspirators, of which Dhvan Singh, the late minister, and Ajeet Singh, a brother of the widow of kurruck Singh (Shere Singh's predecessor) were the heads. The assassination of the monarch was committed by Ajeet Singh; and he shortly afterwards slew his accomplice, Dhvan Singh, whose son (fleers Singh) soon avenged the murder of his sire by the slaughter of Ajeet ! Dhulleep Singh, an alleged son of Kurrtick Singh is on the throne, and Heers Singh has been appointed prime minister ; but the greatest possible anarchy prevails, and perhaps the lives of those now in power are not worth much. The greatest interest is excited in India by this revolution, which, it is expected, will terminate in placing that country, with nearly 4,000,000 inhabitants, and a revenue of upwards of 2,000,000/. sterling, under i he dominion of Ureal Britain. As if it were m anticipation of the events of Lalnre, a large army had been ordered by Lord Ellenhorough to prepare to assemble on the banks of i tie Jumna. Orders were also issued to have a body of Bengal troops sent to occupy IScmde, from whence the Bombay troops were to be withdrawn; hut doubts are now formed of the feasibility of that movement, as all the
Bengal force will be requisite to protect the frontiers against ihe Sikhs. There are It! Out) men now in Scinde. lu the interior of India tranquillity prevails.
